lines.t: Sport, Culture and Society. No exams. Which sounds relaxing, and is actually the trap.
The grade is not built out of exams. It is built out of small, repeated, easy-to-forget tasks. That is good news — if you never miss one.
So we will do the grade first, then the five ideas everything hangs on, then weeks two, three and four in full, then a self-test.
And a word on reflections at the end, because that is where a lot of the points actually live.
Break the grade down.
Eight quizzes at ten points each. Thirteen reflections at ten points each. One final reflection worth twenty — Ultrarealism and Human Flourishment. Plus attendance. No exams at all.
What does a quiz actually test?
The main argument of the readings due that day, plus the lecture slides from the class before. The syllabus says that explicitly, and people still only do the reading.
Now the three ways people lose this grade.
Number one is attendance. After two unexcused absences you lose ten percent of your final grade for every additional class. That is the single biggest risk in the course — bigger than any quiz.
Say that again, because it is the most important sentence in this episode.
Two free absences. After that, ten percent of the final grade, per class. Nothing else in the course moves your grade that fast.
Number two.
Deadlines. Everything is due before class begins. A missed quiz is a zero with no make-up. Late reflections drop a letter grade per day.
And number three, which is the sneaky one.
Not checking email. There are media and current-events assignments that are required and appear nowhere on the syllabus. They arrive by email and Brightspace only.
Is anything recoverable?

Two things. Quiz points you lose can be made up with extra-credit assignments later in the semester. And reflections are self-graded, so a bad week is survivable. But blatantly gaming the self-assessment is treated as cheating.
And a routine, before we get to content.

Twenty-five minutes, four moves. Write the one-sentence thesis of every reading due — if you cannot, you are not ready. Name the evidence, because quizzes are objective questions that reward the study, the place, the number, the person. Re-read the slides from the previous class, one concept per slide. And say the counter-argument out loud.
Why the counter-argument?

Because nearly every reading in this course is arguing against a popular story. Man the Hunter. The ten-thousand-hours rule. Race as biology. If you know the story being attacked, you know the argument.
The five ideas everything hangs on. If someone learns nothing else.
One. Embodiment. Your body is not just biology — it is biology shaped by culture, history and practice, and experienced from the inside. A jump shot, a limp, a fear of the pool. All embodied.
Two.
Biocultural. Refuse the nature-versus-nurture question. The right question is always: how do genes and environment work together here, and how much does each contribute?
Three.
Play, then ritual, then sport. Sport is not an invention of civilisation. It grows out of play, which is older than humans, and it carries ritual meaning. Mayan ball courts were temples.
Four.

Race is a social fact, not a biological unit. Genetic variation is real; races as discrete biological groups are not. Africa holds most human genetic diversity, and that single fact is what collapses the Black athletic gene stories.
And five.
Sport reflects and reproduces power. Gender, race, class and nation are made visible in sport — and made harder to challenge by it. Sport can enrich or stifle, oppress or liberate.
Almost any question in this course can be answered by picking the right one of those and giving an example.

And there are two course capacities to name if a question asks. B is systematic and structural thinking — seeing sport inside larger systems. C is cultural and interpretative investigation — reading difference as meaning, not fact.
One more orienting point.

The course moves outward. Bodies and evolution, then social difference and power, then how anthropologists actually study sport, then character and virtue. Knowing which move you are in tells you what a question is really asking.

lines.chapter: Week 2 — Fox and Konner, why we play
lines.t: Week two. Fox, The Ball, and Konner on play. Argument in one line?
Play looks pointless, costs real energy, and can get you killed — which means evolution kept it for a reason. It builds brains, bodies, and the ability to agree on rules.
Start with the paradox, because the chapter opens on it.

Everyone defines play as useless. Carl Diem called it purposeless activity, for its own sake. Huizinga said it is not serious. Roger Caillois called it an occasion of pure waste — and then spent two hundred pages writing about it. Melvin Konner calls it a central paradox of evolutionary biology.
Stuart Brown's seven characteristics. These are exam-ready.

Voluntary — you are not obliged to do it. Inherently attractive — it is fun. Freedom from time — you lose track of it. Diminished consciousness of self. Improvisational — make-believe, invention. Continuation desire — you never want to stop. And apparently purposeless.
Now the cost side, with numbers.

Young mammals burn up to fifteen percent of their calories playing. And in Peru in nineteen eighty-eight, twenty-two of twenty-six sea pups killed by sea lions were playing in tidal pools and never saw the attack coming.
And the payoff side.
Rats allowed to play developed higher B D N F in the amygdala and prefrontal cortex. And across fifteen mammal species, bigger relative brain size tracked with more play — that is Pellis.
Notice the shape of that argument.
Name the cost, then show a measured benefit. Reuse that shape in your reflections — it is the form the rubric rewards.
Now the dolphins. You said this is the example most likely to be quizzed.
Fox visits Gulf World Marine Park in Panama City Beach to see the psychologist Stan Kuczaj and his rough-toothed dolphins. Three things to remember.
One.

Balls beat everything. In a five-year study of sixteen captive dolphins, they initiated spontaneous play with balls more than with any other object, more than with bubbles, and more than with each other. Fox's phrase is that if play is brain food, ball play is a protein bar. Balls are kinetically interesting — the most animate of inanimate objects — and they are social tools.
Two.
Rules emerge on their own. In ten minutes, free play with Fox became a competitive interspecies ball game with an unspoken but mutually understood set of rules. That is sport in miniature.
Three.
Moderately discrepant events — that is Piaget. Players keep tweaking the rules to make things slightly harder. That is how play sharpens cognition.
And the brain comparison.
Encephalisation quotient. Humans about seven point zero, dolphins about four point five, great apes one point five to three. More brain, more play.
Konner's categories, from the slides.

Two axes. By players and object: solitary locomotor-rotational, object play, social play. And by character: serious, master, rough-and-tumble and adult play. The slides also frame play as behavioural fat — a stored surplus a species can afford, and a guard against hardship.
Two more things from Fox worth a quiz point.

The play deficit. Children spend fifty percent less time playing outdoors than in the nineteen seventies, and ten to sixteen year olds average just twelve point six minutes a day of vigorous activity.
And the throwing hypothesis.

William Calvin, in The Throwing Madonna. Accurate one-armed throwing may have driven lateralisation to the left brain — the same hemisphere that handles the rapid muscle sequencing that language needs. Throwing gave an immediate return, unlike fire or tools. It is speculative. State it, do not defend it.
And why does it matter that hunter-gatherers had leisure?

Richard Lee among the Kung found women could gather three days' food in one day, and Marshall Sahlins said hunters keep bankers' hours. So play is not an invention of civilisation — people have always had the time.
Give me the historical spread, because it is quotable.

Aboriginal marn grook. Copper Inuit akraurak — the aurora borealis is arsarnerit, the football players. Afghan buzkashi. Greek episkyros and ephedrismos. Roman harpastum. And Galen wrote the first scientific case for ball play, praising it as a social leveller: even the poorest man can play ball.
Reflection one is set here. Should play be more serious?

The tension the prompt wants is this. Brown's seventh characteristic says play is apparently purposeless, and yet everything in weeks two and three shows it does serious developmental work. Making play serious — leagues, clinics, travel teams — can destroy exactly the freedom that made it useful. Use the dolphins' backstage game against the ticketed show as your image.
Week three. Ocobock and Lacy. Argument in one line.
Man the Hunter survives because science only studied the traits where males have the advantage. Measured on endurance, female physiology looks at least as well built for hunting.
What is the story being argued against?

The nineteen sixty-six symposium and the nineteen sixty-eight volume Man the Hunter, from Lee and DeVore, made hunting the engine of human evolution — and gave it to men. Laughlin wrote that man's life as a hunter supplied all the other ingredients for achieving civilisation.
And Zihlman's rebuttal, which is the line to memorise.
These pictures of the past are backward projections of modern cultural sex stereotypes onto people who lived a million years ago.
Feminist anthropology answered, but only halfway.

Slocum's Woman the Gatherer in nineteen seventy-five, and Dahlberg's volume in eighty-one. Ocobock and Lacy say that was only half a fix, because it still handed hunting to men. Hrdy's The Woman That Never Evolved went further.
Now the data gap. Three numbers, and this is a favourite quiz fact.

Only thirty-four percent of participants in sport and exercise science research are female. Only fourteen percent in nutritional supplement research. And in athletic performance studies, three percent of publications are female-only, against sixty-three percent male-only.
And the caveat you must always add.
There is more variation within sexes than between them. Every metric overlaps. And sex, like gender, is not a strict binary.
The physiology. Name three reasons females may suit endurance.

Seventy percent greater fatty-acid oxidation, driven by estrogen. Adiponectin up to sixty-five percent higher. More intramuscular fat — fifty-eight against twenty-three grams per kilogram. More Type One fibres. Twenty to thirty-five percent better load-carrying economy. And less exercise-induced muscle damage, so faster recovery.
Now the killer evidence, on distance.
Women and men perform similarly at forty-two kilometres, and women outperform men beyond ninety. One model predicts a female advantage in events of sixty-five kilometres and longer.
And why does that matter for hunting specifically?

Because persistence hunting involves chases of seventeen to thirty-three kilometres. It is endurance, not speed. And Bramble and Lieberman's founding paper on persistence hunting never mentions sex at all.
Two more pieces of evidence.

Pacing — across more than a hundred and ninety thousand runners at the Bolder Boulder ten K, women were one point nine six times more likely to hold pace at halfway. And the ethnography: the Agta of the Philippines, where women hunted with dogs and bows into late pregnancy and returned months postpartum. Also Inuit, Tiwi and Ojibwa.
And the twist at the end, which is the best part of the paper.

Pregnancy and lactation cost about five to six hundred kilocalories a day extra. Motherhood is a multi-year endurance event. So it may be the thing that selected for female endurance — rather than a handicap that ruled women out of hunting.
And the closing image.
Sophie Power running the hundred and sixty-eight kilometre Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc while breastfeeding a three-month-old.
Second half of week three. Epstein, chapters one to three.

Argument in one line. Elite skill is not fast reflexes and it is not ten thousand hours. It is learned pattern recognition — software — running on physical equipment that varies a lot between people — hardware.
Chapter one. Jennie Finch.
The softball pitcher Jennie Finch struck out Albert Pujols, Mike Piazza and Barry Bonds. Alex Rodriguez refused to bat against her.
Was she faster?
No. Her sixty-eight mile an hour underhand pitch from forty-three feet arrives in roughly the same time as a ninety-five mile an hour fastball from sixty feet six inches.
Give me the numbers that explain it.

Simple reaction time is about two hundred milliseconds for everyone — teachers, lawyers, professionals alike. A pitch takes four hundred milliseconds to arrive. The contact window is five milliseconds. So a hitter must commit before the ball is halfway to the plate. Keep your eye on the ball is literally impossible.
And Pujols's own reaction time?
Sixty-sixth percentile against college students. Unremarkable.
So what do experts actually have?

Chunks. Chase and Simon, nineteen seventy-three — grouping information into meaningful patterns. De Groot's chess masters rebuilt real boards from a three-second glance. On random boards, arrangements that could never occur in a real game, their advantage vanished and their recall dropped to average.
And the sport versions.

Janet Starkes' occlusion tests showed the same in volleyball and field hockey. And Bruce Abernethy found that if you hide a badminton player's forearm, an elite player becomes a near-novice. Facing Finch, Pujols had no database. He was a chess master facing a random board.
Chapter two. Two high jumpers.

Stefan Holm — a twenty-year love affair with the high jump, probably more jumps taken than anyone alive, Olympic gold in two thousand four, and an Achilles so stiff it took one point eight tons to stretch it one centimetre. About four times average.
And Donald Thomas.

Took up high jump on a cafeteria bet. Cleared seven feet three and a quarter inches on the seventh jump of his life. Beat Holm at the two thousand seven World Championships with eight months of training — and an unusually long Achilles tendon, ten and a quarter inches. He has not improved a centimetre since.
Now the quiz trap on Ericsson.

K. Anders Ericsson never used the phrase ten-thousand-hours rule. He credits its popularity to a chapter title in Gladwell's Outliers, which he says misconstrued the violin study. That study was cross-sectional and retrospective, on ten pre-screened students. It was not a longitudinal test.
And the strongest evidence against the rule.

Campitelli and Gobet. Chess master level took anywhere from three thousand to twenty-three thousand hours, and some players logged twenty-five thousand and never made master. Epstein's joke is that the seven-thousand-to-forty-thousand-hours rule just does not have the same ring to it.
And chapter three ties it together.

The hardware and software paradigm. Plus talent transfer — the Australian Institute of Sport turned surf-lifesaving and water-skiing athletes into Olympic skeleton racers in fourteen months. And Danish research found late specialisation worked better in centimetre, gram and second sports.
Week four. Epstein, chapters nine to eleven. This is the most careful material in the course.

Argument in one line. Genetic variation is real and it is mostly inside Africa — which is exactly why Black people are built to sprint is bad genetics, even though specific traits with specific histories really do cluster in specific populations.
Chapter nine. Kenneth Kidd.

The Yale geneticist collected D N A worldwide. Every stretch of the genome he looked at had more variation in African populations. On one stretch, a single population of African Pygmies had more variation than the entire rest of the world combined. His line: from a genetic point of view, all Europeans look alike.
And the thought experiment that follows.

For any trait with a genetic component, both the fastest and the slowest person on earth might be African — because African populations hold the greatest diversity, so the extremes at both ends should be overrepresented. Competition only ever looks at one tail.
Now the nuance, because this is where people go wrong in both directions.

Humans are ninety-nine to ninety-nine point five percent identical at the D N A level, and ninety-five percent similar to chimps — but at least fifteen million letters differ between individuals. Similar does not mean unimportant.
And on categories.

Self-identified race matched blind D N A identification in three thousand six hundred and thirty-one of three thousand six hundred and thirty-six Americans. But Kidd and Tishkoff add that with every world population included, the picture becomes a continuous spectrum, not discrete groups.
And it depends on the trait.

About ninety percent of skull-shape variation is within groups. About ninety percent of skin-colour variation is between them. And African Americans range from one percent to ninety-nine percent West African ancestry.
A C T N three. The sprint gene.

Kathryn North was drafting a letter to Nature Genetics announcing a new muscular dystrophy gene — then tested the healthy family members and found they had the same variant. The X variant stops production of alpha-actinin-three in fast-twitch fibres. The R variant makes it.
The distribution.

About twenty-five percent of East Asians and about eighteen percent of white Australians are X X. Under one percent of Zulu, and of African populations generally. And of thirty-two Australian sprinters who reached the Olympics, zero were X X.
So what does the test actually tell you?

Mostly who will not run an Olympic hundred-metre final. North's own caution is that A C T N three contributes a little, there may be hundreds of genes, and diet, environment and opportunity all matter.
And the line to quote.

Carl Foster: if you want to know if your kid is going to be fast, the best genetic test right now is a stopwatch. A C T N three rules out about one billion of seven billion people — and rules out almost no one of African descent.
Chapter ten. Two scientists, opposite conclusions. Set it up as a debate.

Yannis Pitsiladis argues environment and a talent-spotting system. Every Jamaican child sprints on sports day. Champs has run since nineteen ten, a hundred schools, a thirty-five-thousand-seat stadium. Local boosters like Charles Fuller recruit fast kids — he found Sherone Simpson. And both Bolt and Blake originally wanted to play cricket.
And the other side.

Errol Morrison and Patrick Cooper argue a malaria-driven biological history. West African malaria selected for sickle-cell trait and genetically low haemoglobin, and a compensatory mechanism shifted muscle toward fast-twitch fibres — that is Bouchard's nineteen eighty-six Laval study.
Weak spot on each.

Pitsiladis does not explain why the finalists are so consistently of West African descent. And Morrison and Cooper's final step — haemoglobin to fibre type — has never been tested in humans. There is one mouse study and one rat study.
And Pitsiladis has data that kills a romantic theory.

The Maroon warrior theory. Maroons are not genetically distinguishable from other Jamaicans. And one of his graduate students had more sprint gene variants than the likes of a Usain Bolt. His advice to British runners: go into sprinting, do not worry because you are white.
Chapter eleven. What is genuinely established?

Allen's rule on long limbs and Bergmann's rule on narrow build at low latitudes — both help running and jumping. Maximum speed scales with the square root of leg length. And sickle-cell trait protects against malaria, which is Allison, nineteen fifty-four — a textbook evolutionary trade-off.
And its consequences in sport.

Carriers all but disappear from running events over eight hundred metres, and are overrepresented in jumps and throws. Since two thousand, nine Division One football deaths in training were tied to sickle-cell trait, and the N C double-A now screens.
Finally, Cooper's most important point — and this is the one for reflections.

The belief that physical superiority implies intellectual inferiority only developed when physical superiority became associated with African Americans — around nineteen thirty-six. It was a result of bigotry, not a cause of it.
And his answer to the discomfort.
Several scientists told Epstein they have relevant data and will never publish it. Cooper's answer is more careful inquiry, not less.
Self-test. Ten questions, in the style the syllabus describes — main arguments plus the evidence attached to them. Answer out loud.
One. Why could Albert Pujols not hit Jennie Finch?

He had no mental database of her body movements, pitch tendencies or softball spin — no chunks to read. Since a hitter must commit before the ball is halfway, he was left reacting, and raw reaction time is not enough.
Two. What did the random chessboard experiment prove?
That masters' memory advantage is learned pattern recognition, not superior innate memory. On arrangements that could never occur in a real game, their recall dropped to average.
Three. State the strongest evidence against a strict ten-thousand-hours rule.

Campitelli and Gobet: master level took anywhere from three thousand to twenty-three thousand hours, and some players logged twenty-five thousand and never made master. And elite athletes in basketball, field hockey and wrestling average closer to four thousand, four thousand and six thousand sport-specific hours.
Four. Name three physiological reasons females may be suited to endurance.

Any three of: seventy percent greater fatty-acid oxidation; adiponectin up to sixty-five percent higher; more intramuscular fat, fifty-eight against twenty-three grams per kilogram; more Type One fibres; twenty to thirty-five percent better load-carrying economy; less exercise-induced muscle damage; and more consistent pacing.
Five. What is wrong with Man the Hunter, according to Slocum?
A theory that leaves out half the human species is unbalanced. And because the fossil data are so scant, bias fills the gaps with just-so stories.
Six. Why does Kidd say the fastest and the slowest human might both be African?
Because African populations hold the greatest genetic diversity, so for any genetically influenced trait the extremes at both ends should be overrepresented there. Sport only ever measures one end.
Seven. What does A C T N three actually tell you?

Mostly who will not run an Olympic hundred-metre final — the X X genotype is essentially absent among elite sprinters. It rules out roughly one in seven people worldwide, and almost no one of African descent. Foster: use a stopwatch.
Eight. Give the environmental explanation for Jamaican sprinting.

Every child sprints at school sports day. Adult enthusiasts recruit fast kids into track high schools. Champs gives them a thirty-five-thousand-seat proving ground and scholarships. And professional clubs keep them on the island. Talent stays in the sprint pipeline instead of leaking into football as it does in the US.
Nine. What makes the Cooper and Morrison malaria hypothesis only a hypothesis?

The malaria to sickle-cell and malaria to low-haemoglobin links are established. The final step — that low haemoglobin drove a shift toward fast-twitch fibres — has been shown only in one mouse and one rat study, and never tested in humans.
Ten. How does Fox answer his son's question, why do we play ball?

Because play is brain food and balls are the richest kind — kinetically interesting, socially binding objects that build motor skill, cognitive flexibility, and the shared rules that make cooperation possible. It is older than civilisation, not a product of it.
Last thing. Fourteen reflections, self-assessed against a rubric, and no A I in any capacity.
The prompts are explicitly about character, so the V I A framework is the vocabulary the course wants you to use.
Give me the four-move template.

One. Name the concept from the reading, precisely, with the author. Not sports build character — Konner's category of social play. Two. Attach one piece of evidence from the text: a study, a number, a case.
Three.
Bring one thing from your own life, or from this week's sports news. That is why the course requires you to follow current events.
And four, which is the one that separates a good reflection from a filler one.
Say what it costs you. The strongest reflections admit what the idea makes uncomfortable. Then grade yourself honestly against the rubric.
And the V I A strengths, grouped, since reflection four asks about transcendence specifically.

Wisdom — creativity, curiosity, judgment, love of learning, perspective. Courage — bravery, perseverance, honesty, zest. Humanity — love, kindness, social intelligence. Justice — teamwork, fairness, leadership. Temperance — forgiveness, humility, prudence, self-regulation. And transcendence — appreciation of beauty, gratitude, hope, humour and spirituality.
Which is what a stadium does.
Transcendence is the strengths that connect a person to something larger. A stadium, a national team, a ritual ball court — that is exactly the work they do. Which is where the course started.
Go to class. Write the one-sentence thesis. Check your email.
And remember the attendance rule, because it is the only thing here that can quietly cost you a letter grade.
